name: Defence & Trade
whatThisGrades: Federal action on defence spending and trade diversification away from U.S. reliance.
status: NATO's 2% target was met, at 2.01%. Trade is measurably more diversified. The U.S. share of Canadian exports fell from 75.9% to 71.7%. The headline grade is driven mainly by the defence side, with trade tracked separately in the sub-scores below.
verdictLine: The NATO spending target was met, and Canada's trade is measurably more diversified.
judgmentCall: The high grade rests mainly on defence delivery. The trade gains get partial credit, because some of the improvement came from market forces rather than federal policy.
judgmentDetail: The A- is not an endorsement of everything here. Defence spending meets the NATO 2% target, and trade diversification helps the grade. The editor's judgment enters in two ways. First, the trade gain gets only partial credit because the U.S. trade shock itself drove some of the diversification. Second, the grade stops short of an A even though the 3.5% defence-spending path is now funded (Budget 2025, $81.8B over five years). A condition the editor set in advance for raising the defence side was met in the June 2026 review, so that is no longer a reason to hold back. But the grade stayed at A- for two other reasons, and because the trade side is mixed: diversification improved while Canada's overall goods deficit grew to $31.3B in 2025, the largest since 2020. Defence is carrying most of the headline. Trade is tracked separately in the sub-scores below. This review records the first cycle of divergence. If the defence and trade sub-scores move in opposite directions, or differ by more than 1.0 GPA points (about one letter grade), for two consecutive monthly review cycles, the file splits into separate defence and trade grades.
surfaceTags: Trade partly driven by market forces
construct: Whether the federal government met its defence spending commitments and diversified Canada's trade relationships away from heavy reliance on one market.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: The defence target is sustained and trade diversification has materially improved, meaning enough to affect the grade, away from heavy reliance on one market.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting, but not clearly exceeding, the 2% defence floor, and trade diversification that remains partly driven by market forces. The 3.5% target now has a funded path (Budget 2025: $81.8B over five years for the Canadian Armed Forces, or CAF). A pre-set condition for raising the defence side was met in the June 2026 editor review, so that is no longer a discount reason. But the grade held at A- on the two remaining reasons and because the trade half is mixed: diversification improved while the overall goods deficit widened fourfold to $31.3B in 2025.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: The trade war simultaneously creates the diversification problem and drives some of the measured improvement, so trade gains should not be treated as purely policy-caused.

thresholds.criteria: NATO spending is confirmed at or above 2.0% of GDP and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly five points or more, with the diversification holding beyond one-month volatility.
NATO 2% is reached or a funded pathway is in place, and the non-U.S. export share improves by roughly one to five points with corridor, procurement, or agreement execution underway.
Defence spending is rising but still below target, or trade diversification is measurable but modest and not yet durable.
Defence spending is flat or below target and trade dependence on the U.S. is unchanged or worsening.
Defence spending is cut and trade dependence deepens.

scoring.scopeNote: This grade keeps defence delivery and trade diversification together because both sit inside the government's national-security and economic-resilience goals. Read the defence and trade sub-scores alongside the overall grade because the two halves move at different speeds. This grade does not cover the government's broader foreign policy posture, diplomacy, or alliance strategy beyond the published defence and trade-diversification tests.
guardrails: Confirm defence spending from NATO or equivalent official tables, not from domestic political claims alone.
Use annual trade-share movement rather than single-month export volatility when judging diversification.
The defence sub-score anchors the file; trade modifies the headline and should not hide a widening divergence between the two.

If the defence and trade sub-scores move in opposite directions, or differ by more than 1.0 GPA points (about one letter grade), for two consecutive monthly review cycles, the editor will split them into two separate dimensions.

rationale: The government set a specific NATO target, funded it ($81.8B over 5 years), and delivered on timeline. NATO confirmed all allies met the 2% target for the first time in 2025, with Canada at 2.01% in NATO expenditure tables. Trade diversification produced measurable results: U.S. export share fell 4.2 percentage points to 71.7% in 2025, the lowest since the early 1980s, and non-U.S. goods exports rose 17.2% to an all-time high (Global Affairs Canada). The A- rather than A reflects Canada meeting, but not clearly exceeding, the 2% floor. Policy Options flags that the 3.5% GDP defence target is unfunded long term.

name: Major Projects
whatThisGrades: How well the federal system for approving and delivering major infrastructure is working.
status: The Major Projects Office (MPO) is tracking 15 projects in three groups. Four have moved beyond the initial 'designated' stage, and Canada has now initiated the process to list projects under the Building Canada Act. But only 2 show documented progress after being added to the list, and the government has not yet used its power to declare any project a national-interest project.
verdictLine: The Major Projects Office is tracking 15 projects, but only 2 show documented progress so far.
judgmentCall: The grade rests on documented progress after a project is added to the list, not on how many projects were announced or whether any project is a good idea.
judgmentDetail: This grade does not judge whether each project is good policy. It judges the federal delivery process: the 15 projects the Major Projects Office (MPO) is tracking, whether they reached a higher stage on a date after they were added, and whether the government used its national-interest power. The editor's judgment enters in two places. A stage label added on the same day a project joins the list does not count as progress. And a credit-claiming penalty applies where the government overstates its role in projects that were already moving before it stepped in.
construct: How well the federal government's system for approving and delivering infrastructure projects actually works.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: There are 15 projects in the pipeline, but fewer than 30% show progress recorded after being added, and the government's signature national-interest power is still unused.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: Current C includes a credit-claiming penalty. Without that penalty for overstating its role in projects that were already underway, the grade would be a C+.

activeModifiers.name: Credit-claiming penalty
activeModifiers.reason: Most of the projects were already planned by private companies (LNG Canada Phase 2, Crawford Nickel, and others) before the government got involved. It is helping speed them up, not creating them. Independent sources documented that the government overstated its role, which pulls the grade from C+ to C.

activeModifiers.name: Timing Fairness
activeModifiers.reason: Infrastructure takes years and the MPO is still young, but the system itself can already be graded on project-list progress.

thresholds.criteria: At least 50% of the projects show documented advancement of at least 2 stages from 'designated', OR at least one project completes an entire Major Projects Office (MPO) review cycle with a documented timeline improvement compared with before the MPO existed.
At least 30% of the projects show documented progress after being added to the list, with at least one project in approved / permitted / under construction status.
There is a defined set of projects, but fewer than 30% show progress recorded after being added, and no project has completed an entire MPO review cycle. The national-interest power is unused.
A project list exists, but no documented stage progress after being added is visible, OR projects are being withdrawn from the MPO process, OR the framework is being bypassed.
No functioning institutional reform is in place and the federal approval environment worsens versus the inherited baseline.

scoring.scopeNote: This grade is about the federal approval process and project progress, not whether each project is good or bad. Progress is measured against the published stages: designated, reviewed, approved, permitted, under construction, and completed. Only movement recorded after a project enters the list counts toward the grade thresholds.
guardrails: Pre-existing pipeline value does not count as new federal delivery on its own.
A referred project is not the same as a completed MPO review cycle or a verified timeline gain.
Using the national-interest designation or documenting an approval-time improvement is the clearest sign that the federal process is changing outcomes.
Once enough projects reach the permitted / under-construction stages, track median approval time against the MPO's two-year target as the primary acceleration metric.
A project that shows up with a higher stage on the same day it is added does not count as progress until a later stage change is recorded.
scoring.modifierExpiry: Timing Fairness partly applies while the MPO is still inside its first entire project cycle. Until then, institution-building and project-list progress count more than completions, but announcements still do not count as delivery.

rationale: The Major Projects Office is a real institutional change with strong powers under the Building Canada Act (C-5). The official MPO project page now lists 15 referred projects, separate from transformative strategies that are not counted in the project denominator. Of those 15 projects, 4 currently sit above designated status as of May 2026. But only 2 of 15, about 13%, show documented progress after being added to the list: Contrecœur Terminal broke ground April 9, 2026, and Darlington New Nuclear has a later approval / financing milestone. North Coast Transmission Line and Mackenzie Valley Highway have higher stage labels in tranche-announcement sources, but not a later recorded transition after entering the project list, so they are not yet counted toward the B threshold. The remaining 11 projects sit in initial designated status. The national-interest power has never been used. The $126B headline figure mainly represents private-sector investment decisions that already existed. The Fraser Institute and Angus Reid both found the government overstated its role. Documented project-list progress therefore sits well below the 30% threshold for B, so the C grade holds. The credit-claiming penalty scoring adjustment (-0.3 GPA) is reflected in the current C grade. Without the penalty, the grade would be C+, reduced to C based on documented overclaiming of pre-existing projects by Fraser Institute and Angus Reid.

name: Fiscal Health
whatThisGrades: Where the federal budget is headed. Can Ottawa keep up its spending and deficit path without it becoming a problem, and do outside watchers find the plan believable?
status: The Spring Economic Update expects a $66.9B deficit for the 2025-26 fiscal year. The PBO (Parliamentary Budget Officer, Parliament's independent fiscal watchdog) says both fiscal anchors (the government's self-set fiscal targets) are on track. Three open worries hold the grade at C: rising interest costs on the debt, how capital spending is labelled, and defence costs that may not all be counted yet.
verdictLine: Both fiscal anchors are on track, but rising interest costs and other open worries remain.
judgmentCall: The C grade rests on the fiscal anchors (the government's self-set fiscal targets) now looking more believable, with worries still open on the cost of interest, how capital spending is labelled, and defence costs left out so far.
judgmentDetail: The Spring Economic Update and the PBO materially improve the read on where the budget is headed, meaning enough to affect the grade. The deficit-to-GDP anchor is projected to decline and the operating-balance anchor is on track. Judgment still enters in how much weight to give unresolved caveats. The PBO says the capital-budgeting definitions remain imprecise, interest burden keeps rising, and not all anticipated defence spending appears to be reflected.
construct: Whether the federal budget path can keep going without becoming a problem, and whether the plan for the next several years is believable.

gradeBasis.bandCriterion: The deficit sits between 2% and 4% of the size of the economy (GDP). The government has published its deficit-to-GDP and operating-balance fiscal targets, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) currently rates them as on track. But material caveats remain, meaning caveats big enough to affect the grade, on interest burden, capital classification, and whether all defence costs are counted.
gradeBasis.plusMinusRationale: A plain C, no plus or minus. The Spring Economic Update and the PBO fiscal-anchor assessment lift the grade out of D. But the deficit is still above the level needed for a B, and the PBO still flags capital-classification, interest-burden, and defence-cost risks.

activeModifiers.name: External Constraint
activeModifiers.reason: Higher defence spending during the trade war makes strategic sense. But that does not give a pass to other optional spending increases the government chose, such as suspending the gas tax.

thresholds.criteria: The budget breaks even or takes in more than it spends, debt is shrinking as a share of the economy (GDP), the Parliamentary Budget Officer's (PBO) confidence is above 80%, and no credit-rating agency has a warning out.

The deficit is below 2% of the economy's size (GDP), the government has published a multi-year fiscal anchor (a self-set fiscal target), the Parliamentary Budget Officer's (PBO) confidence is between 50% and 80%, and no credit-rating agency has a warning out.

The deficit is between 2% and 4% of the economy's size (GDP), an anchor (a self-set fiscal target) is published but the Parliamentary Budget Officer's (PBO) confidence is only 25% to 50%, or at least one credit-rating agency is flagging a material caveat, meaning a caveat big enough to affect the grade.

The deficit is above 4% of the economy's size (GDP), the PBO's confidence is below 25%, there is no anchor (self-set fiscal target) or it keeps getting missed, and a credit-rating agency is signalling pressure on Canada's rating.
A credit-rating agency actually cuts Canada's rating, or a clear budget crisis takes hold.

scoring.scopeNote: This grades whether the budget path can keep going and whether the plan is believable. It does not grade whether any single spending choice is a good idea.
guardrails: Keep how much debt there is now separate from where the debt is headed. A debt load that looks fine today does not save a path that cannot keep going.
A strategic reason for higher defence spending can explain part of the spending increase, but not the rest of the budget package.

Judge how believable the plan is by what the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO) says about the fiscal anchors (the self-set fiscal targets) and what credit-rating agencies say, not by how the minister describes it.

rationale: The Spring Economic Update lowers the projected FY 2025-26 deficit to $66.9B from Budget 2025's $78.3B, with PBO attributing the improvement mostly to stronger revenues and lower spending. PBO's fiscal-anchor note says the government is on track to respect both anchors: the deficit-to-GDP ratio is projected to decline from 2.1% in 2025-26 to 1.4% by 2030-31, and the operating-balance anchor is projected to be met by 2028-29. That moves this grade out of D. It does not move to B because the deficit remains above the <2% GDP threshold, PBO says the capital-budgeting framework still lacks precision, interest burden rises from 10.6% to 13.2% of revenues by 2030-31, and the projections do not include all anticipated defence spending. Fitch maintained AA+/stable but previously warned that persistent fiscal expansion could raise pressure on Canada's rating over the next several years.

name: Economic Policy Response
whatThisGrades: Federal action to make Canada's economy more productive and competitive. That means investment, innovation, jobs, and wages.
status: Canada's weak productivity (how much it gets out of each hour of work) was inherited, not caused by this government. This grade now tracks four kinds of levers the government can pull: tax, trade, regulation, and funding. But fewer than two of the core levers have reached the authorized or executing stage, and business investment is still close to flat.

status: The consumer carbon price was eliminated, which delivered a campaign promise. verdictLine: The consumer carbon price is gone as promised, but the industrial price is weak in practice.
judgmentCall: The middle grade gives credit for keeping the consumer-price promise, but marks the grade down for the weak industrial price (the price it actually charges per tonne).
judgmentDetail: The C grade keeps two things separate: whether a promise was kept, and how strong the pricing tool is. Removing the consumer charge gets credit as a campaign promise that was carried out. The industrial system gets marked down because the price it actually charges (the effective price signal) is far below the official posted schedule. Judgment comes in by treating the pricing tool as partly intact, but not clearly strong enough to earn a higher grade. The editor fixed the definition on 2026-06-12: the effective-price checks are decided on the marginal compliance price. That is the market price of the compliance credits big emitters buy under the federal Output-Based Pricing System (OBPS) and matching provincial systems, currently about $20 per tonne. It is not the average cost per tonne across the whole economy, which is shown only as background and does not move the grade. Under that definition, the May 15 Canada-Alberta agreement was checked against the $15/t down condition and did not set it off. The agreement weakens the future price path, not the current marginal price.

Democracy Watch calls the ethics screen "loophole-filled," and the House Ethics Committee (ETHI) review of the Conflict of Interest Act in 2026 recommended stronger public reporting and binding directions for conflict-of-interest screens. For a Prime Minister with a background like his, the standard should include a full public accounting reviewed by an independent body.

judgmentDetail: The C grade comes from the published combination rule applied to the five flagship areas. This grade measures delivery capacity, the ability to turn plans into results, not whether defence, housing, major projects, climate, or immigration are good policies. It stays on probation only if the rule runs cleanly through a real cycle, does not contradict the file-status movement underneath it, adds a cross-file execution read beyond any one home card, and clears deconfliction.
